prompt: What did the tribunal decide in *Moffatt v. Air Canada*?

choices.text: The chatbot was a separate entity responsible for itself
choices.why: That was the airline's argument, and it was rejected.

choices.text: It had to honour what its chatbot said
choices.why: Right: what the assistant says is what the company says.

choices.text: The customer should have read the policy page instead
choices.why: The tribunal did not accept that either.

choices.text: Chatbots may no longer answer customers' questions about fares
choices.why: No such rule came out of it.

prompt: Which reasons does the lesson give for treating hallucination as a security issue? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An invented name can be registered by somebody waiting for it
choices.why: Yes: it is exploitable.

choices.text: The assistant's confident voice is read as company policy
choices.why: Yes: it carries authority it has not earned.

choices.text: It cannot be removed inside the model, so checks around it are needed
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Hallucinations leak the system prompt
choices.why: That is a different failure, the subject of another lesson.

prompt: What happened to the lawyers in *Mata v. Avianca*?
hint: They filed what a chatbot produced.

choices.text: Sanctioned for citing decisions that did not exist
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They won, because the chatbot's cases were persuasive
choices.why: The cases had never been decided.

choices.text: The chatbot's provider was fined instead of them
choices.why: The court held the lawyers responsible.

choices.text: Nothing, since nobody checked the citations
choices.why: The judge did check them.

prompt: Why does `guard ground` count `a5`, "I don't know", as a correct answer?
hint: What would a system that punishes it teach?

choices.text: It is the shortest answer in the set
choices.why: Length is not the reason.

choices.text: It beats a guess, and punishing it breeds guesses
choices.why: Right: the question goes to a person instead.

choices.text: Questions about instalments are outside Tarefa's business
choices.why: Nothing says so; the help centre simply does not cover them.

choices.text: The check cannot read answers without citations
choices.why: It read a4 and flagged it.

prompt: `a6` passed every check and is still wrong. What does that show?

choices.text: The help centre page is out of date
choices.why: The page is right; the answer drew the wrong conclusion from it.

choices.text: The number 2 should not have been in the answer
choices.why: The number is right; the event it is counted from is wrong.

choices.text: It matches numbers and names, not meaning
choices.why: Right: a wrong conclusion from the right page passes.

choices.text: Answers that cite one page are always unreliable
choices.why: a1 cites one page and is right.

prompt: How many of the six answers did `guard ground` flag?
An answer is ___ when what it says can be found in the sources it was given.
Why does the lesson want the help centre short, current and unambiguous?
hint: What does a self-contradicting source produce?

choices.text: Short pages cost fewer tokens, and that is the main reason
choices.why: Cost helps; the reason given is about contradictions.

choices.text: Grounded answers then contradict each other
choices.why: Right: the check cannot fix a source that disagrees with itself.

choices.text: Models cannot read pages longer than a screen
choices.why: They can; length is not the issue here.

choices.text: The ANPD requires help centres to be short
choices.why: No such rule.

prompt: Why is a package name a model invented a risk, rather than just a failed install?
hint: Who owns a name nobody has registered?

choices.text: Invented packages install malware automatically
choices.why: Nothing installs by itself; the risk is who registers the name.

choices.text: The name is free for anyone to register
choices.why: Right: the next developer who trusts the suggestion installs their package.

choices.text: Package indexes ban accounts that install missing packages
choices.why: No such rule; a missing package just fails.

choices.text: The model keeps a copy of every invented package
choices.why: The model keeps nothing between calls.

prompt: How many of the five suggested packages are not in the registry snapshot?
Why doesn't `guard deps` check whether `pix-qrcode-br` exists on the public index?

choices.text: It has no network access, and that is the only reason
choices.why: It is a reason; the lesson's point is that the answer would not settle it.

choices.text: Existing would not make it the intended package
choices.why: Right: either way a person reviews it before it is installed.

choices.text: Public indexes do not allow lookups by name
choices.why: They do; that is how a person reviews a package.

choices.text: Only packages with Portuguese names are risky
choices.why: The language of the name has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson recommend for packages a model suggests? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Install from a reviewed list, with versions pinned and hashes checked
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Treat a package name in a model's code as untrusted input
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Watch for the same invented name recurring
choices.why: Yes: that is the name somebody will register.

choices.text: Install the suggestion in a sandbox to see if it works
choices.why: Installing an unknown package is the step that does the damage.

prompt: What does the registry snapshot of this lesson have in common with lesson 9's host allowlist?
hint: Both answer one question about a name.

choices.text: Both check a name a model produced against a list you trust
choices.why: Right: one for the developer's machine, one for the client's browser.

choices.text: Both are maintained by the model provider
choices.why: Tarefa maintains both.

choices.text: Both are only needed for Portuguese text
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Both block the model from answering
choices.why: They block a name from being used, not the answer.

prompt: Put the handling of one assistant answer in order.
items: The model answers and names the documents it used
The code checks that each document exists and each number is in one
A flagged answer is retried once or sent to a person
A passing answer is shown with its source beside it

prompt: The assistant tells a client the refund window is 30 days; the policy says 14. Who answers for it, according to the lesson?

choices.text: The model provider, since its model wrote the sentence
choices.why: The client dealt with Tarefa, as Air Canada's customer dealt with the airline.

choices.text: Nobody, since the answer was generated automatically
choices.why: That argument was made in Moffatt and rejected.

choices.text: Tarefa: its assistant speaks for it
choices.why: Right: which is why the number is checked before it is shown.

choices.text: The client, for not reading the help centre
choices.why: The tribunal rejected that too.

prompt: The real reply `r1` cited all three help centre pages for an answer that came from one. Why did `guard ground` pass it?
hint: What does the check do with a citation?

choices.text: It checks that cited pages exist and hold the numbers, not that each one was needed
choices.why: Right: an unneeded citation is not one it can refuse.

choices.text: A real model's replies skip the check and go straight to the client
choices.why: They went through the same program as the written answers.

choices.text: Three citations count as three votes, and a majority of them agreed
choices.why: Nothing in the check counts votes.

choices.text: The refund page was cited first, and the check reads only the first
choices.why: It joins every cited page that exists.

prompt: The model was asked for one package name per line and replied `pip install qrcode python-cpf`. What does the lesson take from that?
hint: How should a check read a model's output?

choices.text: A check has to read the output as it comes, not as it was asked for
choices.why: Right: which is why `deps.py` drops a leading `pip install`.

choices.text: The model refused the question, so its reply can be ignored
choices.why: It answered; only the format differed.

choices.text: Both names are safe to install, because the model wrote the command itself
choices.why: `python-cpf` is not on the reviewed list.

choices.text: Asking again at temperature 0 would give names one per line
choices.why: At temperature 0 the same question gives the same reply.
